subtype_info: dengue fever complicated by ST-elevation myocardial infarction
title: Dengue fever complicated with ST elevation myocardial infarction with atypical features: A case report
case_text:
A 58 years old female from Western Nepal presented during a dengue outbreak, with complaints of fever for 4 days, myalgia and arthralgia. The fever was intermittent in nature, documented maximum of 102 F, associated with chills and relieved with oral paracetamol. She had multiple episodes of nonbilious, non-projectile vomiting. She also had a history of throat discomfort but without any dysphagia. She gave history of reduced appetite, weakness, fatigue and light-headedness upon standing from a sitting position. There was no history of headache, alteration or loss of consciousness, abnormal body movements, rash, flu-like symptoms, cough, abdominal pain, chest pain, burning micturition, or abdominal distension. Bowel and bladder habits were normal. She has no known comorbidities. She is post-menopausal without a history of tobacco smoking, alcohol abuse, or any other substance use.
On examination, her vitals were within normal limits with blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, pulse of 90 bpm, SpO2 of 95% in room air, respiratory rate of 19 breaths/min, and temperature of 97 F. The findings of systemic examination were within normal limits. Blood investigations revealed total counts of 10,600/mm3, with 85% neutrophils and 12% lymphocytes. Liver function tests were abnormal, with aspartate aminotransferase of 251 U/L and alanine aminotransferase of 300 U/L. Serum sodium was 127 mmol/L and C-reactive protein was positive. She was found positive for dengue NS1 antigen.
Though there were no chest complaints, we performed a routine ECG (Figure 1) to look for any cardiac involvement. The ECG presented ST-segment elevation in leads V3, V4, V5, V6, II, aVF; T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V4, V5, V6; and abnormal Q waves in leads I, aVL, V1 to V6. Troponin I also came back positive. On echocardiography, left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% was noted with anterior wall hypokinesia. With these reports, the diagnosis of STEMI with dengue fever was made. Primary management with loading doses of aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin was done, and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was planned. PCI was done immediately, and 80%-90% stenosis with clot was present in proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD). Stenting with drug eluding stent was done in LAD, and the patient was monitored in cardiac care unit. There were no complications post-procedure, and she was discharged after 8 days of admission on aspirin, atorvastatin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and spironolactone. Her health was improving on subsequent follow-ups without manifestation of any complications.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Dengue
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: dengue fever complicated by ST-elevation myocardial infarction
